\title{What Breaks a Database-and-Documents Assistant, and Which of Its LLM Calls a Cheap Decision Model Can
Replace}

\titlerunning{What Breaks a Database-and-Documents Assistant}
\author{Author names (placeholder)}
\authorrunning{Authors (placeholder)}
\institute{Affiliation (placeholder) \\ \email{email (placeholder)}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
StateSync answers business questions from a company's SQL database, its uploaded filings, or both. On FinanceBench's open sample, the shipped version answered only \N{fbShip} of \N{fbN}
questions correctly. Most of the failures came down to two design decisions: the router saw the 20 most
recently uploaded document titles and nothing about the database, and the answer writer read the first 8 of 25
retrieved passages in filing order. With both fixed, accuracy on this development set
rose to \N{fbBge}, and on a held-out routing test a single front-door LLM call routed \N{rtLLMrawAcc} of
questions correctly, compared with \N{rtShipAcc} for the old router. For SQL, we let a small trained verifier
decide when to distrust the first answer and fall back to a pool of candidates. On \N{sN} held-out BIRD
questions this raised execution accuracy from \N{sFirst} to \N{sPsix} (pre-registered, \N{sH3P}). We also asked
whether Jev, a hosted decision model that returns probabilities rather than text, could take over LLM
calls that only decide something. Zero-shot, it spots wrong SQL answers almost as well as an LLM
judge (AUROC \N{sAurocJev} against \N{sAurocJudge}). Asked a single choice question, it routes without any LLM
call and is not significantly worse than the front door. In a pre-registered test on \N{pgN} held-out
questions, it put the right filing page first \N{pgJBFirst} of the time, against \N{pgBFirst} for a
cross-encoder. It fails when routing is split into separate yes/no questions; we report this and our other negative
results in full.

\keywords{Text-to-SQL \and Retrieval-augmented generation \and Query routing \and Verification \and
Decision models \and Evaluation}
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
More and more assistants that answer business questions sit in front of two kinds of source at once: a database
of figures and a library of documents. Such a system has to work out where a question should go, write the
right query or find the right passage, and ideally notice when its own answer is probably wrong. In most
systems each of these decisions is another large language model (LLM) call, which adds latency and cost and
brings its own ways of failing.

This paper is an account of what we found when we evaluated one such system, StateSync, on questions it had not
been tuned on. On FinanceBench's open questions \cite{islam2023financebench} the shipped version was right only
\N{fbShip} of the time. We traced the failures to specific design flaws, fixed them, and compared each fix with
the version before it. Because we found the flaws on FinanceBench, we did not treat our FinanceBench gains as
evidence. Wherever a question set had been used to find a problem, we built a separate held-out set to test the
fix, and wrote down how it would be analysed before the data existed.

Alongside the fixes we kept asking a second question: which of the system's LLM calls could be handed to
something much cheaper? Several of them write no text that a user ever sees. They only decide something, such as
which source to query or whether an answer looks wrong. We tried Jev \cite{typesafe2026jev} in these roles. Jev
answers typed yes/no and choice questions about a piece of text with probabilities, produces no prose, and costs a
fraction of a cent per call.

The paper makes four contributions.
\begin{itemize}
\item A diagnosis of a document assistant that lost most of its accuracy to a router with too little
information and a writer that read passages in the wrong order. Fixing both raised FinanceBench accuracy from
\N{fbShip} to \N{fbBge}, and one front-door call replaced the two or three LLM calls that used to run before
routing.
\item A detect-then-fallback scheme for SQL. On \N{sN} held-out BIRD questions \cite{li2023bird}, falling back to a
pool of 21 candidate queries only when a trained verifier doubts the first answer raised execution accuracy from
\N{sFirst} to \N{sPsix}. This was one of three pre-registered hypotheses and the only one that survived Holm
correction.
\item Evidence that a decision model can do some of this deciding. Without any training, Jev flags wrong SQL
answers nearly as well as an LLM judge (AUROC \N{sAurocJev} against \N{sAurocJudge}), routes questions without an
LLM call and without a significant loss against an LLM router, and in a pre-registered held-out test puts the right
page at the top of the retrieved passages \N{pgJBFirst} of the time against \N{pgBFirst}. It fails when routing is
broken into independent yes/no questions.
\item A record of what did not work. A ``not answerable'' reply for SQL produced more false refusals than we had
allowed in advance, the fixed system did not significantly beat the shipped one on held-out two-source questions,
and a conformal ``verified'' label never certified a single answer.
\end{itemize}

\section{System}\label{sec:system}
StateSync answers a question from a connected SQL database, from a workspace's uploaded documents, or from both.
Each question takes one of four routes: \emph{sql}, \emph{docs}, \emph{hybrid} (both sources) or \emph{neither},
which gives a polite refusal.

\paragraph{Shipped pipeline.} Before any work on the answer, the shipped system made up to three LLM calls. A
normaliser, written for Hindi and Hinglish questions, passed English text through unchanged; a rewriter turned
every follow-up into a standalone question; and a router chose the route. The router was shown the question and
the titles of the 20 most recently uploaded documents. It saw nothing of the database and none of the other
documents.

\paragraph{SQL route.} An LLM agent reads the schema, writes a query and runs it read-only. If the query fails or
returns nothing, the agent reads a remediation hint and tries again, up to three times. Section~\ref{sec:sql} is
about catching the cases where this first answer is wrong.

\paragraph{Documents route.} A two-round dense search (\texttt{mxbai-embed-large}) first picks the most relevant
documents and then returns up to 25 passages from them. An optional cross-encoder, \texttt{bge-reranker-v2-m3}
\cite{chen2024bgem3}, running on the host GPU, can re-score them. The answer writer reads only the first 8 of the
25, and in the shipped system those 8 were ordered by document and by position within the document rather than by
relevance.

\paragraph{Hybrid route.} An LLM splits the question into a database part and a documents part. In the shipped
system the split only recognised identifiers from the product's original e-commerce domain.

\paragraph{Fixed design.} The fixes, evaluated in Sect.~\ref{sec:docs}, replace the three pre-routing calls with a
single \emph{front door}. It receives the question, the last three turns, a cached \emph{database card} listing
the dataset's tables and columns, and the five documents that best match one dense search. It returns JSON with
the standalone question, whether answering needs the database and whether it needs the documents (yes, no or
unsure for each), whether the question is out of scope, and the split when both sources are needed. A fixed table
turns the two needs into a route, so nothing falls through to SQL by default. The writer now reads passages in
relevance order, each labelled with its filing title and page, and the re-ranker reads the title too. Some hybrid
questions have a documents part that depends on the database part, for example ``which of these companies had
the highest revenue, and what does its annual report say about risks?''. For these, the documents search is
narrowed to filings whose titles name the companies returned by the SQL query.

\paragraph{Jev.} Jev \cite{typesafe2026jev} is a hosted decision model. A request contains a state, which can be
any text, and one or more typed questions. A \emph{noul} question asks whether a statement is true and is answered
with a probability; a \emph{choice} question asks for one of several named options and returns a probability for
each. We called \texttt{jev-1.13} through OpenCode Zen, at \$0.042 per million input tokens. Section~\ref{sec:jev}
covers the seven roles we tried it in.

\section{Method}\label{sec:method}
\paragraph{Development and held-out data.} We kept the data we used to find problems apart from the data we used
to test fixes. FinanceBench's open sample \cite{islam2023financebench}, with 150 questions over 84 SEC filings
(44,918 passages), is our \emph{development} set for the documents route. We diagnosed and fixed the system on
it, so its numbers are not confirmatory. The confirmatory evidence comes from four sets that were built or frozen
before the runs they are used for:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{BIRD held-out} \cite{li2023bird}: \N{sN} questions from the Mini-Dev set, kept out of all
development and scored against corrected gold queries \cite{jin2026annotation}. It is used for the SQL route.
\item \textbf{Routing set}: 224 questions and 24 short conversations over a database of SEC-reported figures for
31 companies and the same 84 filings. Each question is labelled \emph{sql}, \emph{docs}, \emph{hybrid},
\emph{either} (both sources can answer it) or \emph{neither}. We split the set into development and test halves
before any run, made every prompt and threshold choice on the development half, and report the test half
(\N{rtN} questions and \N{rtTurnsN} conversation turns).
\item \textbf{Held-out hybrid set}: 100 two-source questions generated from templates with a fixed seed after the
hybrid design was settled. In 60 of them the documents part depends on the database answer.
\item \textbf{Held-out page set}: \N{pgN} questions that an LLM (Gemini) wrote from randomly sampled filing pages.
FinanceBench's evidence pages and the pages next to them were excluded, and the gold page is the page the question
was written from.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Pre-registration.} For the SQL study, the hybrid set and the page-finding test, we committed the
hypotheses, measures, tests and thresholds to the repository before the data they test existed or had been
scored, and logged every later change. Any analysis we decided on after seeing results is labelled exploratory.

\paragraph{Grading.} SQL answers are scored by executing them and comparing their rows with the corrected gold
under a relaxed comparison. Document answers are graded by an LLM (Gemini 3.8 Flash) against FinanceBench's
answer and justification, with a fixed prompt, in a single shuffled order and without knowing which configuration
produced the answer. The labels are correct, partly correct, incorrect and refused, and we count only
\emph{correct}. Section~\ref{sec:threats} reports a blind check of a random sample of these grades by a second
model.

\paragraph{Statistics.} Paired comparisons use the exact McNemar test, or a sign-flip permutation test when
outcomes are fractional (for example when tied candidates are scored at their expected accuracy). Intervals come
from a bootstrap stratified by database with 2,000 resamples, and within each family of pre-registered hypotheses
we apply Holm's correction.

\paragraph{Run safeguards.} The documents and routing experiments run the product's own code, in containers built
from a recorded commit and kept separate from the shared deployment. The evaluation scripts refuse to run against a
container whose image does not match the recorded build, and they stop if the front door reports that the
database card is missing. We added that second check after a Docker restart left the SEC database stopped and
quietly spoiled an afternoon of routing runs, which we discarded and repeated (Sect.~\ref{sec:threats}).

\section{SQL answers: detect, then fall back}\label{sec:sql}
\paragraph{Candidate pool.} For each of the \N{sN} held-out questions we collected 21 candidate queries: GPT-5
mini's pipeline answer plus five self-consistency samples, the same six from gpt-oss-120b, and three standalone
samples each from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B and GLM-5.3-Flash. Candidates whose results agree form a
cluster. The pipeline's own answer, GPT-5 mini's first candidate, is the \emph{first answer}, and it is correct for
\N{sFirst} of questions. At least one candidate is correct for \N{sOracle}, which is the ceiling for any way of
choosing among them.

\paragraph{Checkers.} We compared four kinds of checker. The first is a ModernBERT-base classifier
\cite{warner2024modernbert}, fine-tuned either on execution-labelled candidates from other questions (``real'') or
on each question's reference query and rule-based mutants of it (``mutation''). The second is Laya, a small
decision model, used zero-shot and fine-tuned. The third is an LLM judge (Gemini 3.8 Flash) that gives a score from
0 to 100. The fourth is Jev, zero-shot, asked ``Does this SQL query and its result correctly answer the
question?''. Every checker sees the question, the query and a preview of its result. The trained checkers are
trained, calibrated and tested on rotating folds stratified by database, so each question is scored exactly once,
by a model that saw neither the question nor the fold used to calibrate its threshold.

\paragraph{Pre-registered hypotheses.} H1: picking the candidate in the pool with the highest ModernBERT score beats
a majority vote. H2: training ModernBERT on real candidates beats training it on mutants. H3: a cascade that keeps
the first answer unless ModernBERT doubts it, and only then picks from the pool, beats the first answer. The doubt
threshold is fitted on the calibration fold in each round.

\centering

fallback policies. Pre-registered comparisons are one-sided and their p values Holm-adjusted; win/loss counts can
be fractional because tied candidates are scored at their expected accuracy.}
\label{tab:sql}
\begin{tabular}{lrl}
\toprule
Policy & Accuracy & Comparison \\
\midrule

ModernBERT-max, mutation (H2) & \N{sPfivem} & real vs mutation, \N{sH2P} \\
\textbf{ModernBERT-triggered cascade (H3)} & \textbf{\N{sPsix}} & +\N{sH3W}/$-$\N{sH3L}, \N{sH3P} \\
ModernBERT score + vote & \N{sPfivev} & exploratory \\
Judge-max & \N{sJudgeMax} & -- \\
Judge-triggered cascade & \N{sJudgeCascade} & -- \\

\paragraph{Results.} Table~\ref{tab:sql} shows that H3 holds. The cascade raises accuracy from \N{sFirst} to
\N{sPsix}, with a 95\% interval for the gain of \N{sPsixCI} points, and it falls back on \N{sPsixFall} of
questions. H1 and H2 point in the expected direction but do not survive the correction. The best policy we found
adds up ModernBERT's scores within each cluster of agreeing candidates and reaches \N{sPfivev}; since we only
thought of it after the pre-registered analysis, it counts as exploratory. The cheaper fallbacks a product team
would probably try first help very little. When the judge doubts the first answer, which happens for
\N{sJudgeDoubts} of questions, re-voting among GPT-5 mini's own samples gives \N{sReVote}, and escalating to
gpt-oss's answer gives \N{sEscalate}.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Detecting a wrong first answer (AUROC, higher is better) and what each checker costs.}
\label{tab:detect}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Checker & AUROC & Training / cost \\
\midrule
LLM judge (Gemini 3.8 Flash) & \N{sAurocJudge} & none; one LLM call per cluster \\
Jev, zero-shot & \N{sAurocJev} & none; \N{sJevCost} for all 6,056 distinct candidates \\
ModernBERT, real & \N{sAurocMB} & 5-fold fine-tuning \\

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Detection.} As Table~\ref{tab:detect} shows, the judge is best at telling when the first answer is
wrong. Jev comes second with no training and a single fixed question, slightly ahead of the fine-tuned ModernBERT,
although the bootstrap intervals for both gaps include zero. Its scores are also stable: when we rescored 200
candidates, the rank correlation with the first run was \N{sJevRetest}. Jev is much weaker at \emph{choosing},
though. Taking whichever candidate it scores highest gives \N{sJevMax}, barely above the first answer.

\paragraph{Jev as the trigger (exploratory).} Since Jev is good at doubting and poor at choosing, we tried it as the
cascade's trigger, with ModernBERT-plus-vote doing the choosing. With Jev's untuned rule of falling back whenever
P(correct)~$<0.5$, accuracy rises to \N{sJthree} (\N{sJthreeP}), and the system falls back on only
\N{sJthreeFall} of questions. With a threshold fitted the same way as H3's it reaches \N{sJtwo}, but it then falls
back on \N{sJtwoFall} of questions. We decided on these analyses after the pre-registered ones, so they are
exploratory.

\paragraph{Approved examples.} A cheaper lever than any checker is to show the SQL writer approved
question--query pairs from the same database, taken from the training folds. We measured this with gpt-oss-120b,
the standalone prompt and three samples per question in each arm. With the product's similarity threshold (E1),
only 54 of the \N{sN} questions get any example at all, and accuracy moves from \N{sExE0} to \N{sExE1}
(\N{sExOneDiff} points, 95\% interval \N{sExOneCI}). Giving the three most similar examples with no threshold (E2)
reaches \N{sExE2} (\N{sExTwoDiff} points, \N{sExTwoCI}). These runs use a different writer from the cascade, so the
numbers cannot be compared directly with Table~\ref{tab:sql}. They do suggest that a set of labelled questions is
worth more as examples for the writer than as training data for a verifier.

\section{Documents and routing}\label{sec:docs}
\paragraph{Diagnosis.} On FinanceBench the shipped system answered \N{fbShip} of questions correctly and declined
\N{fbShipRefused} of the \N{fbN}. Two flaws account for most of this. The first was routing: \N{fbShipToSql} of the
\N{fbN} questions, all of them about documents, went to SQL, even though the FinanceBench workspace's database held
unrelated e-commerce data and could answer none of them. The router saw only the 20 newest of 84 titles and nothing
about the database, so a question about any older filing looked like a database question. The second was what
happened to the \N{fbShipReached} questions that did reach the documents, of which only \N{fbShipReachedCorrect}
were answered correctly. Search often found the right page, but the writer read the first 8 of 25 passages in
document order. The right page was among the 25 for \N{wwDocAny} of questions, yet among the 8 the writer actually
read for only \N{wwDoc}.

\paragraph{Fixes and their effect (development set).} Reading the passages in relevance order raised the share of
questions whose right page reaches the writer from \N{wwDoc} to \N{wwRel}, and adding the re-ranker, with the
filing title included in what it reads, raised it to \N{wwBgeT}. With these changes and the front door in place
of the old router, the system answers \N{fbDense} of FinanceBench correctly without the re-ranker and \N{fbBge}
with it, against \N{fbShip} for the shipped system (+\N{fbBgeW}/$-$\N{fbBgeL}, \N{fbBgeP}). These are
development-set numbers. The confirmatory evidence is in the held-out tests below and in Sect.~\ref{sec:jev}.

\paragraph{Routing (held-out test).} Table~\ref{tab:routing} compares the routers on the test half of the routing
set. Earlier turns are passed exactly as the user typed them, which is what a system that rewrites nothing would
see. The front door routes \N{rtLLMrawAcc} of questions correctly, against \N{rtShipAcc} for the shipped router
(+\N{rtLLMrawvShipW}/$-$\N{rtLLMrawvShipL}, \N{rtLLMrawvShipP}), and \N{rtLLMAcc} when given gold rewritten history
instead. It gets most two-source questions right (\N{rtLLMrawHybrid}) and, unlike the shipped router, declines some
out-of-scope questions (\N{rtLLMrawNeither} against \N{rtShipNeither}). A semantic router, which takes the majority
label of the five most similar labelled development questions, is a strong cheap baseline at \N{rtSemAcc}. It
misses most two-source (\N{rtSemHybrid}) and out-of-scope (\N{rtSemNeither}) questions, though.

\paragraph{Two-source questions (held-out).} On the 100 held-out hybrid questions, an answer counts only if its
database part is right and it cites the right filing. The shipped system gets \N{hyShip}, the fixed system
\N{hyVthree} and the fixed system with entity narrowing \N{hyEnt}. The pre-registered primary comparison, fixed
against shipped, is \emph{not} significant (+\N{hyMainW}/$-$\N{hyMainL}, \N{hyMainP}, two-sided). The
pre-registered secondary comparison is: on the 60 dependent questions, entity narrowing raises the number with
both parts right from \N{hyVthreeDep} to \N{hyEntDep} (+\N{hyEntW}/$-$\N{hyEntL}, \N{hyEntP}). Two weaknesses
hold every arm back. The front door sent \N{hyVthreeToSql} of the 60 dependent questions to SQL alone, and the
database part was right for only \N{hyDbRight} of the 100 questions.

\paragraph{Follow-up questions without an extra LLM call.} The shipped system rewrote every follow-up with an LLM;
we tried replacing that call with simple rules. A turn counts as a follow-up if it contains an anaphor (``it'',
``its'', ``what about'') or names no company, and in that case the last company and year mentioned, looking at the
previous answer first, are carried forward. The models that write the SQL and the answer then receive one extra
line of context. On the routing set's follow-up turns, the rules detect \N{ccDetected} follow-ups with no false
alarms and recover both company and year for \N{ccBoth}. We then answered \N{tuN} turns with gold answers end to
end, routing with Jev's first choice wording. Jev plus the carried context gets \N{tuCarry} right without any LLM
call before routing, against \N{tuNoCtx} with no context (+\N{tuCarryNoW}/$-$\N{tuCarryNoL}, \N{tuCarryNoP}),
\N{tuShip} for the shipped LLM rewriter, and \N{tuLLM} for the LLM front door (+\N{tuCarryLLMW}/$-$\N{tuCarryLLML},
\N{tuCarryLLMP}). The rules recover most of what context is worth, but the front door is still ahead.

\paragraph{A fix that did not ship.} We also let the SQL writer reply ``not answerable'' instead of forcing out a
query. To ship, it had to keep false refusals on 150 answerable held-out BIRD questions at or below 1\%. Three
versions missed that bar, the best with \N{gFalseNA}. Accuracy did not change beyond run-to-run variation: the same
configuration run twice gave \N{gNoiseA} and \N{gNoiseB}. The feature is switched off in every result reported
here.

\section{Jev as a cheap decision layer}\label{sec:jev}
Several of the system's LLM calls produce no text for the user and exist only to \emph{decide} something: whether
an answer is wrong, which source a question needs, which passage holds the answer, or whether a database holds the
data at all. We asked whether a decision model could make these calls instead. Table~\ref{tab:jev} summarises the
seven roles we tried.

in the design; ``dev'' marks development-set or exploratory results.}
\label{tab:jev}

\midrule

Router (one choice) & \N{rtJevCvoneAcc} (first wording), \N{rtJevCAcc} (revised) vs \N{rtLLMrawAcc} for the LLM front door; neither difference significant & held-out (see text) \\
Not-answerable gate & AUROC \N{naAuroc}; \N{naFalse} false refusals, \N{naCaught} unanswerable caught & held-out half, easy negatives \\

\paragraph{Page finding: a pre-registered test.} On FinanceBench, re-ordering the 25 retrieved passages by Jev's
answer to ``Does this passage contain the information needed to answer the question?'' looked promising. Since
FinanceBench is our development set, we set up a confirmatory test. The seed, the filters, the prompts for writing
and checking questions, the arms, the measures and the tests were all committed to the repository before the set
existed. The set has \N{pgN} questions written by Gemini from randomly sampled filing pages, excluding
FinanceBench's evidence pages and their neighbours. Every arm re-orders the same 25 passages, so the arms differ
only in order. The primary hypothesis held. Jev put the right page first \N{pgJBFirst} of the time, against
\N{pgBFirst} for the re-ranker (+\N{pgPoneW}/$-$\N{pgPoneL}, \N{pgPoneP}), and \N{pgJDFirst} when it re-ordered the
dense results alone, without the GPU re-ranker (against \N{pgDFirst} for the dense order). It did not change whether
the right page is among the writer's 8 (\N{pgJBWin} against \N{pgBWin}), which the re-ranker had already brought
close to its ceiling. The gain is therefore in precision: the top passage, which is the one a user is shown as the
source, is right about four times as often. Scoring the 6,220 passages cost \$0.17.

\paragraph{Routing: one choice question works where several yes/no questions fail.} When we asked Jev separate
yes/no questions (``does answering need the database?'' and ``does it need the documents?''), it routed no better
than the shipped router (\N{rtJevYNAcc}) and almost never chose both sources (\N{rtJevYNHybrid} hybrid questions).
Its probabilities show why. On development questions, a question that needs both sources and one that either source
could answer get almost the same pair of scores, so no pair of thresholds can tell them apart. A single choice
question (database only, documents only, both, or neither) makes Jev weigh the sources against each other instead.
We wrote a description of the four options on the development half and ran it once on the test half. It reached
\N{rtJevCvoneAcc}, with every hybrid question right (\N{rtJevCvoneHybrid}), but it sent many documents-only
questions to the database (\N{rtJevCvoneDocs} right), typically ones asking for financial figures the database
does not hold. We then revised the descriptions to say what level of detail the database's columns hold, compared the
two wordings on the development half only, and ran the revision once on the test half: \N{rtJevCAcc}, with documents
at \N{rtJevCDocs}. Because the revision was prompted by errors we had seen on the test half, the first wording's
figure is the cleaner held-out estimate. Against the front door, neither wording differs significantly (first
\N{rtJevCvonevLLMP}, revised \N{rtJevCvLLMP}), and Jev routes in a median \N{rtJevCMs}\,s rather than
\N{rtLLMrawMs}\,s with no LLM call. With \N{rtN} questions these tests could still miss a gap of several points, so
we read them as ``close'', not ``equal''.

\paragraph{A gate for unanswerable SQL questions.} The LLM's ``not answerable'' reply failed its 1\% bar for false
refusals (Sect.~\ref{sec:docs}). We asked Jev ``Does the database described contain the data needed to answer the
question?'' for each of the 150 held-out BIRD questions, once against its own schema and once against the schema
of another, randomly chosen database. With the threshold fitted on one half, the other half had \N{naFalse} false
refusals and \N{naCaught} unanswerable pairs caught. A question put to the wrong database is an easy negative, so
this shows the gate can meet the bar in principle, not that it would on subtler cases.

\paragraph{Where Jev is weak.} Judging whether a written answer is supported by the passages it cites is harder
for Jev. On the fixed system's FinanceBench answers its AUROC is \N{dcAuroc}, too low to be useful as a gate. And,
as Sect.~\ref{sec:sql} showed, it is a good doubter but a poor selector among SQL candidates.

\section{Negative results and threats to validity}\label{sec:threats}
\paragraph{What did not work.} Two of the three pre-registered SQL hypotheses, H1 and H2, did not survive Holm
correction. A conformal ``verified'' label for SQL answers, meant to mark answers with a guaranteed error rate,
did not certify a single answer at either 5\% or 10\%, because the calibration folds were too small for the bound
to be met. The ``not answerable'' reply missed its false-refusal bar and was not shipped. On held-out two-source
questions the fixed system did not significantly beat the shipped one. Jev failed as a router when asked yes/no
questions and was weak as a checker of document answers.

\paragraph{Development-set numbers.} The FinanceBench gains, from \N{fbShip} to \N{fbBge}, were measured on the
same questions we used to diagnose the system and are likely optimistic. The confirmatory evidence for the
documents route is the held-out routing, hybrid and page-finding results.

\paragraph{Test-set reuse in routing.} The routing test half was used more than once. Most routers were fitted on
the development half and run once on the test half, but Jev's revised option wording was written after we had seen
the first wording's test errors (Sect.~\ref{sec:jev}), and we report both.

\paragraph{Generated questions.} The held-out hybrid and page sets were generated, the first from templates and
the second by an LLM, and generated questions may be cleaner than real users' questions. On the page set, a page
other than the source page may also answer a question, which lowers every arm's measured accuracy by the same
mechanism. The LLM that wrote the page questions (Gemini) is also the one that grades document answers, but it
never ranks passages.

\paragraph{Graders.} Document answers are graded by an LLM. To check it, a second model (\textbf{[model name]}),
blind both to the grader's verdicts and to which configuration produced each answer, graded a random sample of 30
answers. It agreed with the grader on 27 of the 30, and on 29 of 30 when only correct versus not correct matters.
All three disagreements involved \emph{partly correct} and a neighbouring label. This is agreement between two
models, not a human check, and we report it as such. SQL answers are scored by execution and need no grader.

\paragraph{A discarded afternoon of runs.} A Docker restart left the SEC database stopped, and for several hours
every front door made its decisions without the database card. We noticed when SQL answers started failing,
discarded the affected runs (they are kept, labelled, in the repository), added a check that stops any run without
the card, and repeated the runs. Every routing number in this paper comes from the repeated runs.

\paragraph{Scope.} The study covers one product, English questions, US public-company filings and one financial
database. Several models were reached through commercial routers that do not disclose their upstream providers,
so we recorded the served model name for every call. Jev is a commercial model and we do not know what it was
trained on.

\section{Related work}
\paragraph{Verification and selection for text-to-SQL.} LEVER \cite{ni2023lever} re-ranks generated programs with a
verifier that reads their execution results. CHASE-SQL \cite{pourreza2025chase} chooses among candidates generated
along several paths with a trained selector, and GradeSQL \cite{tritto2025gradesql} trains outcome reward models
that beat majority voting. Richardson \cite{richardson2026predicts} studies which signals predict whether a query is
correct. Our cascade uses a verifier only to decide \emph{when} to fall back, and we find that a zero-shot decision
model is good at that and poor at choosing.

\paragraph{Cascades and adaptive retrieval.} FrugalGPT \cite{chen2023frugalgpt} escalates to stronger models when a
scorer doubts an answer. Adaptive-RAG \cite{jeong2024adaptiverag} routes questions by their predicted complexity,
and CRAG \cite{yan2024crag} triggers corrective actions based on a retrieval evaluator.

\paragraph{Routing between databases and documents.} Bai et al.\ \cite{bai2025routing} route between structured and
unstructured sources with rules, and find the two complementary and querying both naively expensive. That is why
our front door decides on ``both'' deliberately, from evidence about each source.

\paragraph{Re-ranking.} Cross-encoders such as the BGE family \cite{chen2024bgem3} are the usual second stage of
retrieval. Our page-finding result suggests that a decision model asked a direct relevance question can be a
strong re-ranker when precision at the top matters. We found no published evaluation of Jev on SQL answers,
routing or retrieval.

\section{Conclusion}
When we evaluated a database-and-documents assistant on questions it had not been tuned on, most of its lost
accuracy traced back to two ordinary design choices: what the router was shown, and the order in which the writer
read its passages. Fixing them raised accuracy on our development set from \N{fbShip} to \N{fbBge}; on held-out
data the routing fix held up clearly, while the gain on two-source questions was too small to confirm. We also found that a cheap decision model can take over several of the LLM calls that only make a
decision. It flags wrong SQL answers nearly as well as an LLM judge, routes questions about as well as an LLM front
door when asked a single choice question, and puts the right source page first about four times as often as a
cross-encoder. It breaks down when one decision is split into independent questions, and when it has to judge
prose against evidence. The code, prompts, pre-registrations and every result file are kept with the project
(availability: \textbf{to be decided by the authors}).
